claims.claim: Nearly 30% of αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine were immunogenic, as defined by the detection of surface-bound IgA.
claims.source: Nearly 30% of these αGal+ bacteria were immunogenic (Figure 2D,E), as defined by the detection of surface-bound IgA (Palm et al., 2014), which predominantly targets bacteria in the small intestine (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E, and citations to Palm et al. (2014), Bunker et al. (2017), and Bunker et al. (2015).

claims.claim: IgA+αGal+ bacteria accounted for roughly 50% of all the immunogenic (IgA+) bacteria in the small intestine.
claims.source: These IgA+αGal+ bacteria accounted for roughly 50% of all the immunogenic (IgA+) bacteria in the small intestine (Figure 2D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E), while the percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: The percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E), while the percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Induction of dysbiosis by streptomycin increased the levels of circulating αGal-specific IgM and IgG in Igha-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igha+/+Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Induction of dysbiosis, by streptomycin, increased the levels of circulating αGal-specific IgM and IgG in Igha-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igha+/+Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claims.claim: The IgA response of Ggta1-/- mice reduces systemic IgM and IgG responses against antigens expressed by bacteria in the microbiota.
claims.source: This illustrates again that the IgA response of Ggta1-/- mice is distinct from that of Ggta1+/+ mice, reducing systemic IgM and IgG responses against antigens expressed by bacteria in the microbiota, as illustrated for αGal-like glycans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased systemic IgM and IgG in IgA-deficient mice shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claims.claim: IgA prevents αGal+ bacteria or bacterial products associated to αGal from translocating across epithelial barriers and inducing systemic immune responses against this glycan.
claims.source: Presumably this occurs via a mechanism whereby IgA prevents αGal+ bacteria or bacterial products associated to αGal from translocating across epithelial barriers and inducing systemic immune responses against this glycan.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the reduced systemic antibody responses in the presence of IgA.

claims.claim: Maintenance of microbiota composition across generations is sustained via maternal IgG transfer to the offspring through the placenta during the fetal period, and maternal IgM, IgG and IgA transfer via lactation during the neonatal period.
claims.source: Maintenance of microbiota composition across generations is sustained via maternal IgG transfer to the offspring through the placenta during the fetal period, and maternal IgM, IgG and IgA transfer via lactation during the neonatal period (Gensollen et al., 2016; Koch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gensollen et al. (2016) and Koch et al. (2016).

claims.claim: Over time, newborns generate IgA that target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota, shaping its composition throughout adult life.
claims.source: Over time, newborns generate IgA that target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota (McLoughlin et al., 2016; Moor et al., 2017), shaping its composition throughout adult life (Kawamoto et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLoughlin et al. (2016), Moor et al. (2017), and Kawamoto et al. (2014).

claims.claim: F2 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+, Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/-, Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ and Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice harbored a microbiota composition indistinguishable among the genotypes.
claims.source: Crossing of F0 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ (female) with Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- (male) mice produced F1 Igh-J+/-Ggta1+/-mice, which were interbred to generate F2 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+, Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/-, Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ and Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, harboring a microbiota composition indistinguishable among the genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Maternal Ig transfer predominates over offspring Ig production in shaping the offspring microbiota, regardless of the genotype.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observations (Figure 1C; Singh et al., 2021), this suggests that maternal Ig transfer predominates over offspring Ig production in shaping the offspring microbiota, regardless of the genotype (Ubeda et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the indistinguishable microbiota composition in F2 mice, supported by citation to Ubeda et al. (2012) and Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: There was a marked separation of the microbiota community structure between F3 Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by Principal Coordinate Analyses for Weighted and Unweighted Unifrac.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observations (Figure 1), there was a marked separation of the microbiota community structure between F3 Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by Principal Coordinate Analyses (PCA) for Weighted and Unweighted Unifrac (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Ggta1 deletion shapes both high and low abundant taxa present in the microbiota when maternal and/or offspring-derived antibodies are present.
claims.source: Considering that Weighted Unifrac accounts for the relative abundance of the bacterial taxa while Unweighted Unifrac accounts for only the presence or absence of the taxa in the microbial community (Lozupone and Knight, 2005), they represent differences exerted by high and low abundant bacterial taxa respectively. This suggests that Ggta1 deletion shapes both high and low abundant taxa present in the microbiota when maternal and/or offspring-derived antibodies (i.e. Ig) are present.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA data in Figure 3B and 3C, supported by citation to Lozupone and Knight (2005).

claims.claim: The microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice was enriched in specific bacterial taxa, including Proteobacteria, as compared to the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: LefSe analysis showed that the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice was enriched in specific bacterial taxa, including Proteobacteria, as compared to the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Ggta1 deletion favors gut colonization by pathobionts in an Ig-dependent manner.
claims.source: This suggests that Ggta1 deletion favors gut colonization by pathobionts in an Ig-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of Proteobacteria in Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice.

claims.claim: In the absence of Ig (Igh-J-/-), there were no differences in the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Weighted Unifrac.
claims.source: In the absence of Ig (Igh-J-/-), there were no differences in the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Weighted Unifrac (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Shaping of highly abundant taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs via an Ig-dependent mechanism.
claims.source: This suggests that shaping of highly abundant taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs via an Ig-dependent mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of differences in Weighted Unifrac in the absence of Ig shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained distinct from that of Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Unweighted Unifrac.
claims.source: In contrast, the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained distinct from that of Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Unweighted Unifrac (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Shaping of low abundance bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs in an Ig-independent manner.
claims.source: This suggests that shaping of low abundance bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs in an Ig-independent manner.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistent differences in Unweighted Unifrac even in the absence of Ig shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The Weighted Unifrac distance of microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice was higher than that from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: The Weighted Unifrac distance of microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice was higher than that from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The relative impact of Ig on the gut microbiota community structure exerted by highly abundant bacterial taxa is enhanced in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: This suggests that the relative impact of Ig on the gut microbiota community structure exerted by highly abundant bacterial taxa is enhanced in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the higher Weighted Unifrac distance in Ggta1-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: There was an enhanced Ig-dependent enrichment of several bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice, compared to that of Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: This was confirmed by LefSe analysis showing an enhanced Ig-dependent enrichment of several bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 3E–F), compared to that of Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The Unweighted Unifrac distance of Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice was higher compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: In contrast, the Unweighted Unifrac distance of Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice was higher compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The relative impact of Ig on the microbiota community structure of low abundant bacterial taxa is less pronounced for Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: This suggests that the relative impact of Ig on the microbiota community structure of low abundant bacterial taxa is less pronounced for Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lower Unweighted Unifrac distance in Ggta1-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The gut microbiota from Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking Ig, was enriched with Helicobactereaceae family from Proteobacteria phylum as compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice expressing Ig.
claims.source: In strong support of this notion, the gut microbiota from Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking Ig, was enriched with Helicobactereaceae family from Proteobacteria phylum as compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice expressing Ig (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claims.claim: The gut microbiota of Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking adaptive immunity, is highly enriched in Proteobacteria, including Helicobacter.
claims.source: This is consistent with our previous finding that the gut microbiota of Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking adaptive immunity, is highly enriched in Proteobacteria, including Helicobacter (Singh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: The enrichment of Helicobactereaceae was not observed in Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: Of note, this was not observed in Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The absence of host αGal favors colonization of the gut microbiota by pathobionts, the expansion of which is restrained by Ig.
claims.source: These data suggest that the absence of host αGal favors colonization of the gut microbiota by pathobionts, the expansion of which is restrained by Ig.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of Helicobactereaceae in Ig-deficient Ggta1-/- mice but not in Ggta1+/+ mice.

claims.claim: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against systemic infections by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against systemic infections (i.p.) by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, reflecting a microbiota not shaped by Ig (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Ggta1 deletion enhances protection against systemic bacterial infections via a mechanism involving IgG NAb.
claims.source: This is consistent with our previous finding showing Ggta1 deletion enhances protection against systemic bacterial infections (i.p.) via a mechanism involving IgG NAb (Singh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Moreover, Ggta1-/- mice were also protected against a systemic infection (i.p.) by a cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, reflecting their own Ig-shaped microbiota (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Ggta1-/- mice are protected against cecal ligation and puncture.
claims.source: This is in keeping with the previously shown enhanced protection of Ggta1-/- mice against cecal ligation and puncture (Singh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The IgG-dependent mechanism that protects Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice is distinct from that protecting Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by their own cecal inoculum.
claims.source: This suggests that the previously described IgG-dependent mechanism that protects Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Singh et al., 2021) is distinct from that protecting Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by their own cecal inoculum.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the protection observed in adaptive immune-deficient mice, supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, while succumbing to a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, while succumbing to a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: Lethality from systemic infection with Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- cecal inoculum was associated with a 10^6–10^7-fold increase in bacterial load.
claims.source: Lethality was associated with a 106–107-fold increase in bacterial load (Figure 4C), suggesting that the Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: Lethality was associated with a 106–107-fold increase in bacterial load (Figure 4C), suggesting that the Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential survival and bacterial loads shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: However, Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection (i.p.) with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 4D–E), developing similar bacterial loads (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice developed similar bacterial loads upon infection with cecal inocula from Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: However, Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection (i.p.) with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 4D–E), developing similar bacterial loads (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The mechanism via which the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice shapes and reduces the pathogenicity of its microbiota is not operational in Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.source: This suggests that the mechanism via which the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice shapes and reduces the pathogenicity of its microbiota is not operational in Ggta1+/+ mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of differential pathogenicity in Ggta1+/+ mice shown in Figure 4D-F.

claims.claim: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells using an anti-GR1 monoclonal Ab increased the susceptibility of Ggta1-/- mice to systemic infection by their cecal inoculum.
claims.source: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells (i.e. polymorphonuclear cells and inflammatory monocytes) using an anti-GR1 monoclonal Ab (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; Daley et al., 2008) increased the susceptibility of Ggta1-/- mice to systemic infection by their cecal inoculum (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, and citation to Daley et al. (2008).

claims.claim: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells was associated with a 10^2–10^5-fold increase in bacterial load, compared to control Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: This was associated with a 102–105-fold increase in bacterial load, compared to control Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Monocyte/macrophage depletion by Clodronate liposomes failed to compromise the survival of Ggta1-/- mice upon infection by the cecal inoculum.
claims.source: Of note, monocyte/macrophage depletion by Clodronate liposomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G; Sunderkötter et al., 2004) failed to compromise the survival of Ggta1-/- mice upon infection by the same cecal inoculum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, and citation to Sunderkötter et al. (2004).

claims.claim: Polymorphonuclear cells are essential for resistance against systemic infection emanating from the less pathogenic Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.source: This suggests that polymorphonuclear cells are essential for resistance against systemic infection emanating from the less pathogenic Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of neutrophil vs. macrophage depletion shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection but can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan.
claims.source: While loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection, these can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan, as illustrated by the occurrence of reproductive senescence upon Ggta1 deletion in mice (Singh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Reproductive senescence occurs upon Ggta1 deletion in mice.
claims.source: While loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection, these can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan, as illustrated by the occurrence of reproductive senescence upon Ggta1 deletion in mice (Singh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutations in glycosyltransferase genes are rare, and in some cases unique, to the human lineage.
claims.source: In an evolutionary context, such a trade-off could explain why loss-of-function mutations in these genes are rare, and in some cases unique, to the human lineage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning about the rarity of such mutations.

claims.claim: Loss of CMP-N-acetylneuraminic acid hydroxylase (CMAH) function eliminated expression of the sialic acid, N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), in humans.
claims.source: The latter is illustrated by the loss of CMP-N-acetylneuraminic acid hydroxylase (CMAH) function, which eliminated expression of the sialic acid, N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), in humans (Ghaderi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ghaderi et al. (2011).

claims.claim: Co-evolution of ancestral hominids with commensal bacteria in their microbiota is thought to have provided a series of fitness advantages including optimization of nutrient intake from diet, regulation of different aspects of organismal metabolism or colonization resistance against pathogenic bacteria.
claims.source: Co-evolution of ancestral hominids with commensal bacteria in their microbiota (Dethlefsen et al., 2007; Huttenhower et al., 2012; Moeller et al., 2016), is thought to have provided a series of fitness advantages including, among others, optimization of nutrient intake from diet, regulation of different aspects of organismal metabolism or colonization resistance against pathogenic bacteria (Buffie and Pamer, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dethlefsen et al. (2007), Huttenhower et al. (2012), Moeller et al. (2016), and Buffie and Pamer (2013).

claims.claim: The loss of αGal expression, as it occurred during primate evolution, might have exerted a major impact on the nature of symbiotic associations with the microbiota.
claims.source: Here we propose that the loss of αGal expression, as it occurred during primate evolution, might have exerted a major impact on the nature of these symbiotic associations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings in mice.

claims.claim: Mutations altering the expression of human ABO blood group glycans are associated with shaping of the bacterial composition of the gut microbiota.
claims.source: While our studies do not provide direct evidence that the loss of αGal played a major role in shaping the microbiota composition of Old- vs. New World primates, this notion is supported, indirectly, by the recent finding that mutations altering the expression of human ABO blood group glycans are associated with shaping of the bacterial composition of the gut microbiota (Rühlemann et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rühlemann et al. (2021).

claims.claim: Host 'αGal-like' glycans shape the microbiota composition of mice and primates, including that of humans.
claims.source: In light of the structural similarity between the human B blood group (i.e. Galα1-3(Fucα1-2)Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-R), and αGal (i.e. Galα1-3Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-R) glycans, our findings probably reflect a general mechanism whereby host 'αGal-like' glycans shape the microbiota composition of mice and primates, including that of humans.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural similarity and experimental findings.

claims.claim: A relatively large proportion of probiotic bacteria as well as bacteria present in the mouse microbiota express αGal-like glycans at the cell surface.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, a relatively large proportion of probiotic bacteria as well as bacteria present in the mouse microbiota express αGal-like glycans at the cell surface (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: About 30% of αGal+ bacteria carry IgA at the cell surface in the mouse microbiota and are considered as immunogenic.
claims.source: About 30% of these carry IgA at the cell surface in the mouse microbiota and, as such, are considered as immunogenic (Palm et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2 and citation to Palm et al. (2014).

claims.claim: Ggta1 deletion probably broadens bacterial recognition by IgA to include immunogenic αGal+ bacteria, which are presumably eliminated.
claims.source: This suggests that Ggta1 deletion probably broadens bacterial recognition by IgA to include immunogenic αGal+ bacteria, which as a result are probably purged from the microbiota.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the reduced proportion of IgA+αGal+ bacteria in Ggta1-/- mice.

claims.claim: IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity.
claims.source: Of note, these are not mutually exclusive possibilities since: (i) IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity (Hamadeh et al., 1995), (ii) IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015) and (iii) αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes (Bernth Jensen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamadeh et al. (1995).

claims.claim: IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria.
claims.source: Of note, these are not mutually exclusive possibilities since: (i) IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity (Hamadeh et al., 1995), (ii) IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015) and (iii) αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes (Bernth Jensen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bunker et al. (2017) and Bunker et al. (2015).

claims.claim: αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes.

claims.claim: Ggta1 deletion in mice increases resistance to bacterial sepsis via two distinct antibody-dependent mechanisms: one involving a relative increase in antibody effector function when αGal is not present in the biantennary glycan structures of IgG, and another relying on shaping and reduction of the microbiota pathogenicity by antibodies, most likely from the IgA isotype.

The first involves a relative increase in antibody effector function, when αGal is not present in the biantennary glycan structures of IgG (Singh et al., 2021). The second relies on shaping and reduction of the microbiota pathogenicity by antibodies, most likely from the IgA isotype.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis of findings supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021) and data from the current study.

results.result: Ggta1 deletion shapes gut microbiota composition across generations. The microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice differs from Ggta1+/+ mice, with increased Proteobacteria, Tenericutes, and Verrucomicrobia, and decreased Bacteroidetes and Deferribacteres. This divergence emerges by F3 generation and is influenced by environmental pathobiont colonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C23-C34 are supported by comprehensive 16S rRNA sequencing data across multiple generations (Figures 1A-F, Figure 1 supplements 1-4). The breeding strategy controls for environmental factors while allowing genotype effects to emerge. The data show consistent, reproducible differences in microbiota composition that develop over generations.

results.result: Despite increased Proteobacteria in Ggta1-/- mice, there is no associated pathology. Histological examination and fecal lipocalin-2 measurements show no inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract or other organs, suggesting maintained symbiotic homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by histological data (Figure 1 supplement 3A-C) and biochemical measurements (Figure 1 supplement 3B). The absence of pathology despite altered microbiota composition is well-documented. However, the inference of 'maintained symbiotic homeostasis' (C28) is reasonable but could benefit from additional functional assays.

results.result: Ggta1 deletion enhances microbiota-specific IgA responses without altering total IgA levels. This enhancement is microbiota-dependent and occurs partly through T-cell-dependent mechanisms. The enhanced IgA response is specific to bacteria present in Ggta1-/- microbiota.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C43 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 2A-B, Figure 2 supplement 1A-D) and germ-free colonization experiments. The distinction between total and microbiota-reactive IgA is well-controlled. The T-cell dependence is demonstrated using Tcrb-/- mice. The specificity for Ggta1-/- microbiota is shown through cross-colonization experiments.

results.result: Approximately 20% of bacteria in the mouse small intestine express αGal-like glycans, with ~30% of these being immunogenic (IgA+). IgA+αGal+ bacteria account for ~50% of all immunogenic bacteria. Ggta1-/- mice have reduced IgA+αGal+ bacteria while maintaining similar total IgA+ bacteria levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2C-E, Figure 2 supplement 2) using BSI-B4 lectin staining for αGal and anti-IgA antibodies. The quantification is clear and reproducible. The reduction of IgA+αGal+ bacteria in Ggta1-/- mice while maintaining total IgA+ bacteria suggests specific targeting of αGal-expressing bacteria.

results.result: IgA in Ggta1-/- mice reduces systemic IgM and IgG responses against microbiota antigens. Dysbiosis induction in IgA-deficient Ggta1-/- mice increases circulating αGal-specific IgM and IgG, suggesting IgA prevents bacterial translocation and systemic immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 2F-G) comparing Igha-/- and Igha+/+ mice. However, C53 is speculative about the mechanism. While the data support that IgA reduces systemic responses, the proposed mechanism of preventing translocation is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. Additional experiments tracking bacterial translocation would strengthen this claim.

results.result: Ggta1 deletion shapes microbiota via Ig-dependent and Ig-independent mechanisms. Highly abundant taxa are shaped via Ig-dependent mechanisms (shown by Weighted Unifrac), while low-abundance taxa are shaped independently of Ig (shown by Unweighted Unifrac). The Ig-dependent effect is enhanced in Ggta1-/- compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C70 are supported by comprehensive breeding experiments using Igh-J-/- mice and beta-diversity analyses (Figure 3A-F, Figure 3 supplement 1). The distinction between Weighted and Unweighted Unifrac appropriately captures abundance-dependent vs. presence/absence effects. The experimental design controls for maternal transmission effects. The statistical analyses (PERMANOVA) are appropriate.

results.result: In the absence of Ig, Ggta1-/- mice show enrichment of Helicobacteraceae (Proteobacteria), which is restrained by Ig. This enrichment is specific to Ggta1-/- mice and not observed in Ggta1+/+ mice, suggesting αGal absence favors pathobiont colonization that is controlled by Ig.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by LEfSe analysis (Figure 3E-F, Figure 3 supplement 1D) and consistent with prior work (C72, Singh et al. 2021). The genotype-specific effect (C73) strengthens the interpretation. However, C74 is an inference that, while reasonable, would benefit from additional mechanistic studies to confirm the proposed relationship between αGal absence, pathobiont colonization, and Ig control.

results.result: Ggta1-/- mice are protected against systemic infection by both Ig-shaped and non-Ig-shaped microbiota. Surprisingly, this protection persists in mice lacking B cells, T cells, or both, suggesting distinct protective mechanisms: IgG-dependent protection against non-Ig-shaped microbiota versus an alternative mechanism against Ig-shaped microbiota.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 are supported by survival data (Figure 4 supplement 1A-E). The protection in adaptive immune-deficient mice (C79-C81) is surprising and well-documented. The inference of distinct mechanisms (C82) is logical given the differential requirements for adaptive immunity depending on microbiota source. However, the exact nature of the alternative mechanism requires further investigation.

results.result: Ig-shaped microbiota from Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic than non-Ig-shaped microbiota. Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice survive infection with Ig-shaped microbiota but succumb to non-Ig-shaped microbiota, with lethality associated with 10^6-10^7-fold higher bacterial loads.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by survival curves and CFU quantification (Figure 4A-C). The dramatic difference in bacterial loads provides strong evidence for reduced pathogenicity. The experimental design appropriately controls for host genotype while varying microbiota source. This is a key finding demonstrating functional consequences of Ig-mediated microbiota shaping.

results.result: The mechanism by which adaptive immunity shapes microbiota to reduce pathogenicity is specific to Ggta1-/- mice. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice show similar susceptibility to infection regardless of whether the microbiota is Ig-shaped or not.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by survival and CFU data (Figure 4D-F). The lack of differential pathogenicity in Ggta1+/+ mice provides important negative control data. However, the sample size appears limited (n=4-5 per group) compared to other experiments. Additional replicates would strengthen confidence in this genotype-specific effect.

results.result: Neutrophils (Ly6C+/Ly6G+ cells) are essential for resistance against systemic infection by Ig-shaped microbiota in Ggta1-/- mice. Neutrophil depletion increases susceptibility and bacterial loads by 10^2-10^5-fold, while macrophage depletion has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by depletion experiments with survival and CFU data (Figure 4G-H, Figure 4 supplement 1F-H). The differential effects of neutrophil vs. macrophage depletion are well-controlled and clearly demonstrate neutrophil-specific requirement. The flow cytometry confirms successful depletion. This identifies the innate immune mechanism underlying protection against low-pathogenicity microbiota.

results.result: Ggta1 deletion shapes microbiota through multiple mechanisms: Ig-dependent shaping of abundant taxa (involving maternal and offspring-derived IgA, IgM, IgG) and Ig-independent shaping of low-abundance taxa (possibly through altered nutritional/spatial niches at epithelial barriers).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C112-C115 synthesize findings from multiple experiments. The Ig-dependent mechanism is well-supported by data in Figures 2-3. However, C113 and C115 are largely speculative about specific mechanisms (maternal antibody transfer, mucus glycan alterations). While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations, they lack direct experimental validation in this study. The claims appropriately use qualifying language ('presumably', 'probably').

results.result: Ggta1 deletion increases resistance to bacterial sepsis through two distinct antibody-dependent mechanisms: (1) enhanced IgG effector function when αGal is absent from IgG glycans, and (2) IgA-mediated shaping of microbiota to reduce pathogenicity, with protection mediated by neutrophils rather than adaptive immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C121-C123 integrate findings from the current study with prior work (Singh et al. 2021). The two-mechanism model is well-supported: mechanism 1 is established by prior work (C123 cites Singh 2021), while mechanism 2 is demonstrated by current data (Figures 2-4). The shift from adaptive to innate immune dependence for Ig-shaped microbiota is clearly shown. This represents a major conceptual advance.

results.result: The authors propose that GGTA1 loss-of-function mutations in ancestral primates may have been selected partly due to reduced microbiota pathogenicity through antibody-mediated shaping, providing fitness advantages against sepsis that contributed to fixation of these mutations during primate evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C98, C100, C119, C127, C132, C135 are evolutionary inferences extrapolating from mouse data to primate evolution. While the mouse data are solid, the evolutionary claims are speculative. The authors appropriately use qualifying language ('may have', 'probably', 'suggests'). However, direct evidence for this mechanism in primates is lacking. The claims rely on structural similarity between αGal and ABO blood group glycans (C99-C100) and assume similar mechanisms operate across species, which is uncertain.

results.result: Maternal antibody transfer and offspring IgA production maintain microbiota composition across generations. In Ggta1-/- mice, adaptive immune pressure allows establishment of diverse ecosystems containing pathobionts, whose expansion is restrained by Ig, explaining the absence of pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are well-supported by citations. Claims C116-C118 integrate experimental findings with mechanistic inferences. The enrichment of pathobionts in Ig-deficient Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 3E-F) and absence of pathology in Ig-sufficient mice (Figure 1 supplement 3) support this model. However, C117 about antibodies targeting other symbionts is speculative. The overall model is reasonable but some mechanistic details remain to be validated.

results.result: Loss-of-function mutations in glycosyltransferase genes can provide fitness advantages against infection but may compromise physiologic functions of eliminated glycans. Such mutations are rare in humans, exemplified by GGTA1 and CMAH losses, reflecting evolutionary trade-offs.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by citations to prior work. C93-C94 cite Singh et al. 2021 for reproductive senescence in Ggta1-/- mice. C96 cites Ghaderi et al. 2011 for CMAH loss. C97 cites multiple papers on microbiota co-evolution. These are well-established facts from the literature used to contextualize the current findings. C95 is a reasonable inference about evolutionary constraints.

results.result: The mechanism of microbiota shaping likely involves IgA targeting of αGal-expressing bacteria. Human ABO blood group glycans similarly shape microbiota. Multiple bacterial species express αGal-like glycans, including E. coli O86:B7, which can induce protective αGal-specific antibody responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C101-C102, C107-C111 are supported by citations and experimental data (Figure 2C, Figure 2 supplement 2). C103 is a reasonable inference from the reduced IgA+αGal+ bacteria in Ggta1-/- mice, though the mechanism remains somewhat speculative. C104-C106 cite literature on IgA polyreactivity. The overall model is well-supported, though direct demonstration of IgA binding to bacterial αGal would strengthen the mechanism.

results.result: Host-microbiota interactions are dynamic, shifting between symbiotic and pathogenic states. Sepsis imposes high fitness costs in humans, suggesting mutations reducing microbiota pathogenicity provide fitness advantages. Primates show high sepsis susceptibility, possibly reflecting trade-offs between resistance and disease tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C131 are supported by citations to relevant literature. C124-C125 cite papers on host-microbe dynamics. C126 cites sepsis mortality data. C128-C131 cite papers on primate immunity and resistance-tolerance trade-offs. These claims provide important conceptual framework for interpreting the findings. The logic connecting these concepts is sound, though the specific application to GGTA1 evolution remains speculative.

results.result: Background context on glycosyltransferases under selection pressure, infectious disease as a driver of natural selection, GGTA1 loss in primate evolution, sepsis pathogenesis, microbiota fitness costs/benefits, immune system evolution, and IgA function in microbiota shaping.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C22 provide background knowledge supported by extensive citations to established literature. These are not novel findings but rather contextualize the current work. C1 lacks specific citations but represents general knowledge. All other claims are well-supported by appropriate references. These establish the scientific foundation for the study.

results.result: Prior work showed that αGal absence from IgG Fc glycans increases IgG effector function and resistance to bacterial infections. This survival advantage came with reproductive senescence as a fitness cost, presumably outweighed by pathogen exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 cite Singh et al. 2021 for both the IgG mechanism and reproductive senescence. These are established findings from prior work that motivate the current study. The inference about fitness trade-offs (C134) is reasonable but speculative regarding the balance between costs and benefits in evolutionary context.
